title: Professional Scrum Master I (PSM I) Study Guide
description: Professional Scrum Master I (PSM I) is Scrum.org's evidence that you understand Scrum as the Scrum Guide defines it and can apply it on a real team. The assessment is 80 questions in 60 minutes with an unusually high 85% pass mark, taken online whenever you are ready, and costs $200 per attempt. It draws on three competency areas: understanding and applying the Scrum framework, developing people and teams, and managing products with agility.
audience: Scrum Masters and aspiring ones, delivery leads, developers and product people who want the framework straight from its source, and anyone on a team that says it does Scrum and would like to know what that should mean. No prerequisites and no course attendance required — which is the point: unlike the CSM, this credential is awarded for passing an assessment, not for sitting in a classroom.
why_get_it: PSM I is widely regarded as the more rigorous of the two mainstream Scrum Master certifications. Unlike the Scrum Alliance CSM, which requires a mandatory paid course (typically $400–$1,000+) and renewal fees every two years, PSM I has no course requirement and is valid for life—you pay $200 for the assessment and that is the entire cost, forever. The exam itself has teeth: an 85% passing score across 80 questions in 60 minutes means you cannot pass on vibes and buzzwords. That rigor is exactly why hiring managers who know the agile certification landscape respect it. It demonstrates you understand empiricism, the Scrum events and artifacts, self-managing teams, and what the Scrum Master accountability actually is (hint: not a project manager with a new title). For BAs, coordinators, and developers on agile teams, it is a low-cost way to formalize working knowledge; for aspiring Scrum Masters, it is the standard entry credential.
when_to_get_it: Take PSM I when you need the credential quickly and cheaply, or when you want to prove you know the framework rather than that you attended a class. Read the Scrum Guide properly — it is short and the assessment is drawn from it — then use the free Scrum Open practice assessment until you are scoring comfortably above 85%, because the real thing gives you 45 seconds a question. The comparison people ask about is the CSM: it requires a paid two-day course and renewal every two years, while PSM I costs $200, needs no course and never expires. The trade-off is that CSM's course-plus-network suits people who want the teaching; PSM I suits people who want the certificate.
salary_note: This range reflects U.S. Scrum Master and agile delivery roles broadly, not a PSM I premium—the certification alone does not move salary the way experience does. Entry-level and career-changer candidates with PSM I but no Scrum Master experience typically land coordinator or team-level roles first. Experienced Scrum Masters and agile coaches in major markets frequently exceed $110K, but that is driven by track record, with the cert acting as a filter-passer.
exam_format: 80 questions in 60 minutes, 85% to pass: multiple choice, multiple answer and true/false. Taken online on your own computer, unproctored, with no test centre and no appointment. Available in English, Japanese and Simplified Chinese. Your assessment password never expires but is valid for one attempt only.
recertification_note: PSM I is a lifetime certification: no renewal fees, no continuing education, no re-assessment, and a free Credly digital credential. That is a genuine differentiator against the CSM, which requires paid renewal every two years.

study_steps.title: Read the Scrum Guide—then read it again
study_steps.description: The 2020 Scrum Guide is roughly 13 pages and it is the source of truth for the exam. Read it at least five times over your study period. PSM I questions hinge on exact wording: who attends which event, what is a commitment versus an artifact, what the Scrum Master is accountable for. Casual familiarity fails this exam; precise knowledge passes it.

study_steps.title: Take the free Scrum Open assessment until you score 100% consistently
study_steps.description: Scrum.org publishes the Scrum Open, a free practice assessment drawn from the same knowledge areas as PSM I. Take it repeatedly until you score 100% every single time, quickly. This is the community-standard benchmark: if you cannot ace the Open assessment without hesitation, you are not ready for the real exam, which is significantly harder.

study_steps.title: Unlearn common Scrum misconceptions
study_steps.description: Most wrong answers on PSM I come from real-world habits, not lack of study. If your workplace treats Sprints as mini-waterfalls, the Scrum Master as a project manager, or the Daily Scrum as a status report to management, the exam will punish those instincts. For every rule in the Scrum Guide, make sure you understand why it exists—the reasoning is what lets you answer scenario questions correctly.

study_steps.title: Drill scenario-based practice questions
study_steps.description: The real exam leans on 'what should the Scrum Master do in this situation?' questions where several answers look plausible. Practice question banks (Udemy practice tests are the popular paid option) train you to spot the answer that aligns with the Scrum Guide rather than with common workplace practice. Review every wrong answer against the Guide's actual text.

study_steps.title: Practice your exam pacing
study_steps.description: 80 questions in 60 minutes is 45 seconds per question. The exam is unproctored and technically open book, but there is no time to look things up—if you plan to search the Scrum Guide mid-exam, you will run out of clock. Use the bookmark feature: answer everything, flag uncertain questions, and return to them at the end.

study_steps.title: Buy the assessment password and take the exam when ready
study_steps.description: Purchase the PSM I assessment directly from Scrum.org for $200. There is no test center and no scheduling—you receive a password and take the exam online whenever you are ready (the password does not expire). If you took an official Scrum.org PSM course, you get a free second attempt if you take the exam within 14 days of receiving your password and do not pass. Self-studiers pay $200 per attempt, so go in prepared.

faq.question: PSM I vs CSM — which should I get?
faq.answer: PSM I (Scrum.org) costs $200, requires no course, and never expires. CSM (Scrum Alliance) requires a mandatory two-day course typically costing $400–$1,000+, and requires paid renewal every two years. The PSM I exam is also harder—85% passing bar versus CSM's more lenient exam. If you are self-studying and cost-conscious, PSM I is the better value. CSM's advantage is the live instruction and, in some organizations, existing name recognition. Most hiring managers who know the agile space treat PSM I as equal or more rigorous.

faq.question: Is PSM I worth it?
faq.answer: For $200 with lifetime validity, the cost-to-value ratio is among the best in certifications. It gets you past resume filters for Scrum Master and agile delivery roles and formalizes knowledge for BAs, coordinators, and developers on agile teams. Be honest with yourself about the limits: it proves you understand Scrum, not that you can run a team. Employers hiring Scrum Masters weight experience heavily, so pair the cert with real agile team exposure.

faq.question: How hard is the PSM I exam?
faq.answer: Harder than its entry-level reputation suggests. You need 85% (roughly 68 of 80 questions correct) in 60 minutes—about 45 seconds per question. Many questions present several plausible answers where only one aligns with the Scrum Guide's exact wording. Candidates who rely on workplace 'Scrum' experience without studying the Guide fail regularly. With focused study, most candidates are ready in 2–4 weeks.

faq.question: Do I need to take a course to sit PSM I?
faq.answer: No. There are no prerequisites and no mandatory training—this is a key difference from the CSM. You can buy the $200 assessment password and self-study using the free Scrum Guide and Scrum Open assessment. Scrum.org does offer official PSM courses, and course attendees who fail a first attempt within 14 days of receiving their password get a free second attempt, but the course is entirely optional.

faq.question: Does PSM I expire?
faq.answer: No. PSM I is valid for life with no renewal fees and no continuing education requirements. This is unusual in the certification world—most competing credentials (including CSM) require periodic paid renewal.

faq.question: Will PSM I get me a Scrum Master job?
faq.answer: On its own, usually not. Scrum Master openings typically ask for agile team experience, and the cert is the filter, not the qualifier. Realistic paths: get PSM I while working as a BA, developer, tester, or coordinator on an agile team, volunteer for Scrum Master duties internally, and use that combination to move into the role. Career changers with PSM I but zero agile exposure should target agile team-member or project coordinator roles first.

faq.question: What comes after PSM I?
faq.answer: Scrum.org offers PSM II (proven ability to apply Scrum in complex situations) and PSM III (distinguished-level mastery), plus specialized assessments like PSPO (Product Owner track) and PAL (agile leadership). Outside Scrum.org, PMI's CAPM or ITIL 4 Foundation broaden your delivery credentials, and experienced practitioners often move toward agile coaching rather than collecting more certs.

related_certs.title: PMI CAPM
related_certs.reason: The entry-level project management credential. CAPM now includes agile content, and pairing it with PSM I covers both traditional and agile delivery for coordinator and PM-track roles.

related_certs.title: ITIL 4 Foundation
related_certs.reason: The service management counterpart to PSM I. Together they signal fluency in how modern IT organizations both run services and deliver change.

related_certs.title: ISTQB CTFL
related_certs.reason: For testers and QA professionals on Scrum teams, CTFL plus PSM I formalizes both the testing craft and the agile context it operates in.
